### Problem: Submatrices that sum to target {#sec-mat-p4-submatrix}

::: {.p-statement}
Count the non-empty submatrices (contiguous rectangles) of an $m \times n$ matrix whose elements sum to `target`.

$1 \le m, n \le 100$, $-1000 \le$ cell $\le 1000$, $-10^8 \le$ target $\le 10^8$. On `[[0,1,0],[1,1,1],[0,1,0]]` with target $0$ the answer is $4$ (the four $1 \times 1$ zero cells). On `[[1,-1],[-1,1]]` with target $0$ the answer is $5$ (two $1 \times 2$, two $2 \times 1$, one $2 \times 2$).

Source: [LC 1074 · Number of Submatrices That Sum to Target](https://leetcode.com/problems/number-of-submatrices-that-sum-to-target/){.solved difficulty="Hard"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Fix the top and bottom rows and the band between them collapses to one array of column sums; a rectangle with those rows is exactly a contiguous run of that array (@sec-mat-a5). So the 2-D count becomes, for each of the $O(m^2)$ bands, the 1-D "count subarrays with sum $=$ target", which a prefix-sum hash map answers in $O(n)$.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Four nested loops.** Enumerate top, bottom, left, right and sum the rectangle cell by cell — the definition, and the oracle.
2. **Integral image.** Build the 2-D prefix table of @sec-pref-2d once; then every rectangle sum is one inclusion–exclusion query, but there are still $O(m^2n^2)$ rectangles.
3. **Fix two rows, collapse to 1D.** For each `top`, grow a column-sum array `col` row by row as `bottom` moves down. For each band, sweep its prefix sums $S$ and add `cnt[S - target]` before inserting $S$ — the 1-D kernel of Subarray Sum Equals K (@sec-pref-p2-a), seeded with `cnt[0] = 1`.

**Invariant.** A subarray $(l, r]$ of `col` has sum $S_r - S_l$, so when the sweep is at $r$, `cnt[S_r - target]` is exactly the number of left ends $l < r$ whose rectangle (rows `top..bottom`, columns $l..r-1$) sums to target.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Four nested loops

::: {.form-next}
Enumerate $(\text{top}, \text{bottom}, \text{left}, \text{right})$ and sum the rectangle directly. $O(m^2 n^2)$ time with the sum recomputed each time — far too slow as written for $100 \times 100$, but it is the definition, and the oracle every faster rung is checked against.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("submatrix", "brute")
    assert str(final) == "4"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def sub_brute(M, target):
    m, n = len(M), len(M[0])
    cnt = 0
    for top in range(m):
        for bottom in range(top, m):
            for left in range(n):
                for right in range(left, n):
                    s = sum(M[i][j] for i in range(top, bottom + 1) for j in range(left, right + 1))
                    if s == target:
                        cnt += 1
    return cnt


assert sub_brute([[0, 1, 0], [1, 1, 1], [0, 1, 0]], 0) == 4
assert sub_brute([[1, -1], [-1, 1]], 0) == 5
assert sub_brute([[1]], 1) == 1
assert sub_brute([[1]], 0) == 0
```

##### C++

```cpp
long long subBrute(vector<vector<int>>& M, int target) {
    int m = M.size(), n = M[0].size();
    long long cnt = 0;
    for (int top = 0; top < m; ++top)
        for (int bottom = top; bottom < m; ++bottom)
            for (int left = 0; left < n; ++left)
                for (int right = left; right < n; ++right) {
                    int s = 0;
                    for (int i = top; i <= bottom; ++i)
                        for (int j = left; j <= right; ++j) s += M[i][j];
                    if (s == target) ++cnt;
                }
    return cnt;
}
```

:::

#### Integral image (2-D prefix)

::: {.form-next}
Build `P[i+1][j+1] = M[i][j] + P[i][j+1] + P[i+1][j] - P[i][j]`, then any rectangle sum is one inclusion-exclusion query `P[b+1][r+1] - P[t][r+1] - P[b+1][l] + P[t][l]`. The four loops remain, but the innermost work drops from $O(\text{area})$ to $O(1)$, so the rung is $O(m^2 n^2)$ *time* with $O(mn)$ space — the natural bridge from "recompute the sum" to "don't."
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("submatrix", "prefix")
    assert str(final) == "4"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def sub_prefix(M, target):
    m, n = len(M), len(M[0])
    P = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(m + 1)]
    for i in range(m):
        for j in range(n):
            P[i + 1][j + 1] = M[i][j] + P[i][j + 1] + P[i + 1][j] - P[i][j]
    cnt = 0
    for t in range(m):
        for b in range(t, m):
            for l in range(n):
                for r in range(l, n):
                    if P[b + 1][r + 1] - P[t][r + 1] - P[b + 1][l] + P[t][l] == target:
                        cnt += 1
    return cnt


assert sub_prefix([[0, 1, 0], [1, 1, 1], [0, 1, 0]], 0) == 4
assert sub_prefix([[1, -1], [-1, 1]], 0) == 5
assert sub_prefix([[1, 2], [3, 4]], 3) == 2
```

##### C++

```cpp
long long subPrefix(vector<vector<int>>& M, int target) {
    int m = M.size(), n = M[0].size();
    vector<vector<long long>> P(m + 1, vector<long long>(n + 1, 0));
    for (int i = 0; i < m; ++i)
        for (int j = 0; j < n; ++j)
            P[i + 1][j + 1] = M[i][j] + P[i][j + 1] + P[i + 1][j] - P[i][j];
    long long cnt = 0;
    for (int t = 0; t < m; ++t)
        for (int b = t; b < m; ++b)
            for (int l = 0; l < n; ++l)
                for (int r = l; r < n; ++r)
                    if (P[b + 1][r + 1] - P[t][r + 1] - P[b + 1][l] + P[t][l] == target) ++cnt;
    return cnt;
}
```

:::

#### Fix two rows, collapse to 1D

::: {.form-next}
The rung the pattern names. For each `top`, keep a `col[j]` array and widen `bottom`, adding row `bottom` into it — a $O(1)$-per-column update, not a re-derivation. Then count subarrays of `col` equal to `target` with a prefix **hash map**: `total += cnt[pre - target]` *before* `cnt[pre] += 1`, seeded by `cnt[0] = 1`. This is one loop shorter than the integral image: $O(m^2 n)$ time, $O(n)$ space.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("submatrix", "collapse")
    assert str(final) == "4"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
from collections import defaultdict


def sub_collapse(M, target):
    m, n = len(M), len(M[0])
    total = 0
    for top in range(m):
        col = [0] * n
        for bottom in range(top, m):
            for j in range(n):
                col[j] += M[bottom][j]
            cnt = defaultdict(int)
            cnt[0] = 1
            pre = 0
            for v in col:
                pre += v
                total += cnt[pre - target]
                cnt[pre] += 1
    return total


assert sub_collapse([[0, 1, 0], [1, 1, 1], [0, 1, 0]], 0) == 4
assert sub_collapse([[1, -1], [-1, 1]], 0) == 5
assert sub_collapse([[1, 2], [3, 4]], 3) == 2
assert sub_collapse([[900, 700], [500, 500]], 1000) == 1
for _ in range(30):
    m, n = random.randint(1, 4), random.randint(1, 4)
    M = [[random.choice([-2, -1, 0, 1, 2]) for _ in range(n)] for _ in range(m)]
    for tgt in (-2, 0, 1, 3):
        assert sub_collapse(M, tgt) == sub_brute(M, tgt) == sub_prefix(M, tgt)
```

##### C++

```cpp
long long subCollapse(vector<vector<int>>& M, int target) {
    int m = M.size(), n = M[0].size();
    long long total = 0;
    for (int top = 0; top < m; ++top) {
        vector<int> col(n, 0);
        for (int bottom = top; bottom < m; ++bottom) {
            for (int j = 0; j < n; ++j) col[j] += M[bottom][j];
            unordered_map<int, int> cnt;
            cnt[0] = 1;
            int pre = 0;
            for (int j = 0; j < n; ++j) {
                pre += col[j];
                total += cnt[pre - target];
                ++cnt[pre];
            }
        }
    }
    return total;
}
```

:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
Let $m \le n$ (swap dimensions if not). **Four nested loops** is $O(m^2 n^2 \cdot m n)$ — hopeless at $100 \times 100$. **Integral image (2-D prefix)** is $O(m^2 n^2)$ time, $O(mn)$ space. **Fix two rows, collapse to 1D** is $O(m^2 n)$ time, $O(n)$ space: $O(m^2)$ row-pairs each solved in $O(n)$ by the hash map. On $100 \times 100$ that is roughly $10^6$ versus the integral image's $10^8$ — the collapse rung is the intended solution.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- `target` may be negative and cells may be negative, so prefix sums are *not* monotone — you must use the hash map, not the sliding window of @sec-sw (which needs non-negative values).
- A single row reduces the problem to plain 1-D subarray-sum-equals-k; the collapse loop runs once with `top == bottom == 0`.
- `cnt[0] = 1` is not decoration: without it, subarrays that start at column $0$ (whose prefix equals `target`) are never counted.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- **Counting `cnt[pre - target]` after inserting `cnt[pre]`.** When `target == 0` this would match a prefix with itself and add a phantom empty subarray. Always read the count, then insert.
- **Re-summing `col` from scratch per bottom row.** The `col[j] += M[bottom][j]` update is what makes the rung $O(m^2 n)$; recomputing the column band each time silently reintroduces the inner $O(m)$ and turns it back into the integral-image cost.
- **Sliding window on negative values.** A two-pointer window only works when all values share a sign; with negatives the prefix sums go down as well as up, and only the hash map stays correct.
:::

**Variants.** Subarray Sum Equals K (@sec-pref-p2-a) is the 1-D kernel this form wraps, and Range Sum Query 2D (@sec-pref-p4-a) is the integral image answering rectangle sums in $O(1)$. Max Sum of Rectangle No Larger Than K (@sec-mat-p4-nolarger) keeps the same band loop and swaps the hash map for a sorted set. [CF 1323B · Count Subrectangles](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1323/B){rating="1500"} collapses differently: its matrix is $c_{ij} = a_i b_j$, so an all-ones rectangle is a run of ones in $a$ times a run of ones in $b$, and the 2-D count factors into two 1-D counts.

**Try it.** Maximise instead of counting: return the largest rectangle sum (the 2-D Kadane of @sec-mat-a5) by replacing the hash map with a running minimum prefix.
